name: Technology & Media
tagline: Screens, software, streaming and the social web
blurb: The highest-frequency cluster in the 2026 forecast: eight Part 2 cue cards, four Part 1 frames and seventeen Part 3 questions all draw on a single lexical set and a single stock of arguments.

vocab.def: to be watching a screen so intently that you notice nothing else
vocab.n: Mildly critical and faintly humorous. Safe when describing other people; when describing yourself, soften it with I'm guilty of… so it does not read as self-reproach.
vocab.eg: My younger brother is glued to a screen from the moment he wakes up.

vocab.def: the compulsive reading of distressing news online, long past the point of usefulness
vocab.vi: lướt tin xấu không dứt ra được
vocab.n: A genuinely recent coinage and therefore strong evidence of a wide lexical resource. Use it once; repeating it dilutes the effect.
vocab.eg: I deleted the app because I would end up doomscrolling until two in the morning.

vocab.def: a deliberate period spent away from phones and computers
vocab.vi: kỳ nghỉ khỏi thiết bị số
vocab.n: Neutral to slightly informal; equally at home in Part 1 and Part 3. Collocates with go on and do, not with make.
vocab.eg: Every few months I go on a digital detox — no social media for a fortnight.

vocab.def: the length of time a person can concentrate on one thing
vocab.n: Semi-academic and precise. The standard collocations are a short attention span and a shrinking attention span.
vocab.eg: Short-form video has done real damage to our collective attention span.

vocab.def: so well designed that it can be used without instruction
vocab.vi: dễ dùng đến mức không cần hướng dẫn
vocab.n: The upgrade path is easy to use (Band 6) → user-friendly (Band 7) → intuitive (Band 8). Same idea, markedly different lexical value.
vocab.eg: What sold me on the app was how intuitive the interface is — nothing needs explaining.

vocab.def: to remove the remaining faults from a system before release
vocab.vi: xử lý nốt các lỗi còn lại
vocab.n: Informal and idiomatic; a natural choice when narrating a technical failure in Part 2.
vocab.eg: They pushed the update out before they had ironed out the bugs, and the whole thing froze.

vocab.def: (of a device) to work erratically without failing completely
vocab.n: British and conversational. Weaker than crash, which implies total failure — the distinction is worth making audible.
vocab.eg: My laptop had been playing up for weeks before it finally gave up on me mid-presentation.

vocab.def: to spread very rapidly across the internet
vocab.n: Neutral. Note the fixed form: go viral, never become viral. Collocation errors of this kind are exactly what examiners register under Lexical Resource.
vocab.eg: The clip went viral overnight, which was the last thing she had expected.

vocab.def: an environment in which people encounter only opinions that mirror their own
vocab.n: A heavyweight Part 3 item. Reserve it for discussion of algorithms, polarisation and public opinion; it will sound forced in Part 1.
vocab.eg: Algorithms quietly build an echo chamber around you, so you only ever hear your own opinion repeated.

vocab.t: take something with a pinch of salt
vocab.def: to treat a claim with reasonable scepticism
vocab.vi: nghe mà vẫn giữ hoài nghi
vocab.n: Informal but widely used in serious speech. American English substitutes grain for pinch; either is accepted.
vocab.eg: Anything trending on social media I take with a pinch of salt until a proper outlet confirms it.

vocab.n: Positive in tone and ideally suited to questions about the benefits of technology. Avoid pairing it with a negative clause; the register clashes.
vocab.eg: You have the entire library of human knowledge at your fingertips, which previous generations simply did not.

vocab.def: to set an upper limit on hours spent using devices
vocab.vi: đặt giới hạn thời gian dùng màn hình
vocab.n: Neutral and policy-flavoured. Cap and limit are interchangeable here; cut down on is the informal alternative.
vocab.eg: Parents are right to cap screen time, but banning devices outright tends to backfire.

vocab.def: to be so absorbed in something that you cannot stop
vocab.n: Stronger than enjoy but lighter and less clinical than be addicted to. A cheap and effective way to stop repeating I like.
vocab.eg: I got hooked on a Korean crime series and finished all sixteen episodes in a weekend.

vocab.def: something that brings disadvantages alongside its benefits
vocab.n: The natural hinge for a balanced Part 3 answer. Mind the pronunciation: the w in sword is silent, and mispronouncing it undercuts an otherwise sophisticated phrase.
vocab.eg: Remote learning is a double-edged sword: it widens access, but it isolates the students who need contact most.

vocab.def: skilled and confident in using technology
vocab.n: Complimentary and informal. The polite negative is not particularly tech-minded rather than bad at technology.
vocab.eg: My grandmother is surprisingly tech-savvy — she video-calls us more often than we call her.

vocab.def: to make the distinction between two things harder to see
vocab.n: Academic in register. Productive across topics: work and home, real and virtual, reporting and opinion.
vocab.eg: Social media has blurred the line between reporting and simply airing an opinion.

vocab.def: to stop thinking about work or problems and relax
vocab.vi: ngắt kết nối, thư giãn đầu óc
vocab.n: The literal sense (turning a device off) is Band 6 vocabulary; the figurative sense used here is what earns credit.
vocab.eg: I find it almost impossible to switch off if my phone is anywhere in the room.

vocab.def: something that provides essential support in a difficult period
vocab.n: Emotionally weighted. Best kept for genuinely serious contexts — isolation, distance, illness — where the weight is earned.
vocab.eg: During those months apart, a ten-minute video call every evening was an absolute lifeline.

p1.q: Do you spend too much time on social media?

b6.h: A clear answer, extended enough to be assessable
pts: Answer in the first clause. Restating the question wastes the seconds in which the examiner forms a first impression.
Two or three sentences is the target. A single-clause reply gives the examiner nothing to rate.
Common vocabulary is acceptable at this level provided the meaning is unambiguous.

b7.h: A qualified answer with one less common item
pts: Avoid absolutes. A condition — it depends on how busy the week is — signals control rather than indecision.
Insert one less common collocation per answer, not four. Density of idiom is not what the descriptor rewards; accuracy is.
Use natural discourse markers such as to be fair and having said that in place of moreover and furthermore, which belong to written English.

b8.h: A position of your own, expressed with precision
b8.f: Reframe → Personal stance → Vivid specific → Understated close
pts: Interrogate the question before answering it: what would actually count as too much?
Include one detail so specific it could not have been memorised — a number, an app name, a time of day.
Let the closing clause carry a light, dry judgement. Restraint reads as fluency; emphasis reads as rehearsal.

p2.q: Describe a problem of technology you have encountered

b6.h: Cover all four prompts and reach the time
pts: Answer the bullet points in order. They exist precisely to prevent you from running out of material.
Give each bullet two or three sentences.
If you finish early, return to the final bullet and add how you felt. Stopping under one minute costs you on Fluency and Coherence regardless of accuracy.
Open with a specific moment, not with I would like to talk about, which announces rehearsal.
Use narrative tenses deliberately: past continuous for background, past perfect for what had already happened.
Include one line of direct speech. It forces a change of intonation and immediately animates the account.

b8.h: Build tension, vary the pace, land on meaning
b8.f: In medias res → Rising tension → Pause → Payoff → Broader reflection
pts: Delay the resolution by one beat. Anticipation is what distinguishes a story from a report.
Vary sentence length by function: short clauses at the crisis, longer ones in reflection.
Close on an observation that outlives the anecdote. So that was my experience forfeits the ending.

p3.q: Do you think people depend too much on technology nowadays?

b6.h: Take one side and defend it
pts: State the position in the opening clause.
Two reasons, each with an example, is sufficient structure at this level.
Do not attempt both sides unless you can hold them apart; half-argued balance reads as self-contradiction.
Grant the opposing view before answering it: there is some truth in that, but…
Introduce a category: by age group, by sector, or by degree. Categorisation is visible reasoning.
Close on a condition — provided that… — rather than a flat verdict.

b8.h: Reframe the term, separate the cases, forecast
b8.f: Reframe → Distinguish → Counter-example → Trade-off → Conditional forecast
pts: Separate dependence from over-dependence. Drawing a conceptual distinction is among the clearest markers of Band 8 reasoning.
Supply a counter-example of your own rather than one from a textbook.
Frame the issue as a trade-off rather than as right and wrong.
End on a conditional forecast; slogans close an answer, arguments open outwards.

critical.q: Do you think people depend too much on technology nowadays?

for.h: The case that we are over-dependent
for.main: Technology has displaced capacities that people once had to hold themselves, and the loss of those capacities is real rather than nominal.
sup: Deskilling. Almost nobody can now recall a phone number or read a paper map. A skill that goes unused does not lie dormant; it atrophies.
Single points of failure. One network outage can halt a hospital and an airport alike. Dependence without a fallback is not convenience but exposure.
Cognitive cost. Attention spans have contracted, and with them the willingness to sit with a difficult problem long enough to solve it.

against.h: The case that this is simply specialisation
against.main: Every generation has depended on its instruments; that is how civilisations accumulate capability rather than evidence of decline.
sup: Historical precedent. Plato held that writing would ruin human memory. The complaint now reads as quaint, and today's version may age no better.
Released capacity. Offloading mechanical recall frees attention for analysis and judgement, which is where human advantage actually lies.
Distinguish the cases. A surgeon relying on imaging is specialised; a teenager unable to sleep without a phone is dependent. Collapsing the two into one word is a failure of argument, not a finding.

critical.verdict: The Band 8 resolution: the issue is not how heavily we lean on technology but whether anything remains to fall back on when it fails. Dependence with redundancy is efficiency; dependence without it is fragility.

models.q: Do you think people depend too much on technology nowadays?
models.html:
Yes, I think so. People today use technology for almost everything, and I think it is too much. For example, when my phone is not working, I cannot go anywhere because I don't know the way. I always use Google Maps.

Another reason is that people don't talk to each other. When my family has dinner, everyone is looking at their phone. It is not good for relationships. So I think yes, we depend too much on technology.

notes.fc: The position is clear and the answer is organised, but the connectives are few and repeated — precisely the descriptor for Band 6, which credits a range of markers used though not always appropriately.
notes.lr: The resource is sufficient to convey the meaning, and no item is wrong; nothing, however, is less common. Not good, too much, cannot are all high-frequency choices.
notes.gr: Simple sentences with a subordinate when clause. No relative clause, no conditional, no inversion. Errors are absent chiefly because nothing ambitious is attempted.
notes.pr: Stress falls on content words and the speaker is comfortably intelligible, but the rhythm is even and intonation flattens across the turn — control is variable.

models.prosody: YES, I think so. // People toDAY use techNOlogy for ALmost EVerything ↘
models.tip: This answer is safe, and its ceiling is 6.0. One concession would lift it towards 6.5: Having said that, in some fields it is actually a good thing.

models.q: Do you think people depend too much on technology nowadays?
models.html:
I'd say we do, though it depends enormously on the situation. In everyday life, a lot of us have outsourced skills we used to take for granted — I couldn't navigate my own city without a map app, and I'd struggle to recall more than two phone numbers.

Having said that, I don't think that's automatically a bad thing. If technology frees up mental space, that energy can go into work machines can't do. The problem, as I see it, is the lack of a backup. When a system goes down, whole hospitals or airports simply grind to a halt, and it's that fragility that worries me, rather than the dependence itself.

notes.fc: The turn is sustained without visible effort and the markers vary in function — concession, attribution, contrast. This is the flexibility the Band 7 descriptor requires. One mid-sentence hesitation remains, but coherence is unaffected.
notes.lr: Outsourced skills, take for granted, free up mental space, grind to a halt, fragility. Less common items are present and stylistically appropriate, with awareness of collocation.
notes.gr: Error-free sentences are frequent: a second conditional, a temporal clause, a cleft construction. The range is real, though not yet used with complete freedom.
notes.pr: Chunking is sensible and contrastive stress lands on backup and fragility. Intonation is not yet varied across the whole turn, which is what separates this from Band 8.

models.prosody: I'd say we DO, / though it dePENDS eNORmously‿on the situAtion ↗ // In EVeryday life, / a lot of us have OUTsourced skills / we used‿to take for GRANted ↘
models.tip: Three links to rehearse: depends‿enormously, used‿to realised as /juːstə/, and goes down with the /z/ carrying into /d/.

models.q: Do you think people depend too much on technology nowadays?
models.html:
It hinges on what we mean by 'too much', I think — because dependence and over-dependence get lumped together far too casually. A surgeon who relies on imaging isn't dependent in any troubling sense; she's specialised. A teenager who can't fall asleep without a phone under the pillow is something else entirely.

What I'd argue is that the real question isn't how much we lean on technology, but whether there's anything to fall back on when it fails. Had our grandparents lost their calculators, they'd have reached for a pencil; lose the network today and a hospital stops functioning. That's not dependence, that's brittleness.

And to be fair, every generation has panicked about this — Plato was convinced that writing would rot our memories, which reads as rather quaint now. So I'd resist the doom-laden version of the argument. Provided we keep the fallbacks alive, I'd call it a reasonable trade rather than a problem.

notes.fc: The architecture is visible without being announced: definition, central claim, historical concession, conditional verdict. Pauses occur, but they prepare content rather than retrieve language — the distinction the Band 8 and 9 descriptors turn on.
notes.lr: Hinge on, get lumped together, fall back on, brittleness, doom-laden, quaint. Idiomatic items are deployed skilfully and the register shifts consciously into dry understatement.
notes.gr: Conditional inversion (Had our grandparents lost…), an imperative functioning as a conditional (lose the network today and…), and a non-defining relative clause. Structures change according to rhetorical need and the majority of sentences are error-free.
notes.pr: Contrastive stress is used argumentatively on dependence / over-dependence and again on dependence / brittleness. The falling contour on rather quaint now carries the irony. This is phonology conveying meaning, not merely accurate articulation.

models.prosody: It HINges‿on what we mean by 'too much' ↗ / I think — // because dePENdence / and Over-dependence / get lumped toGEther far too CASually ↘ ‖ (pause 0.4s) A SURgeon who relies‿on Imaging / isn't dependent‿in‿any TROUbling sense ↗ / she's SPEcialised ↘
models.tip: The most valuable phonological move here is the contrast between DE-pendence and O-ver-dependence. If the two are not audibly different, the entire argument collapses. Drill the pair ten times before recording.
